extracted.intended_audience: authors, editors, compositors, and typesetters preparing books/journal articles for publication
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and conventions for hyphenation, footnotes, indexing, tables, spacing, indentation, headings, proofs, and other typographical matters for book and journal composition. Intended as an editorial/typesetting reference to produce correctly formatted printed matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liquid-consonant hyphenation rule
rubrics_metrics.description: The liquid consonants l and r, when preceded by any consonant other than s, must not be separated from that consonant, except in uniting parts of compound words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ha-blar, po-dria, ce-le-bra-ci-on, si-glo; but sub-lu-nar, sub-ra-yar, es-la-bon. Preserve the consonant+liquid cluster together when dividing syllables, except at compound-word boundaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separable-consonant and s-separation rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Two separable consonants should be divided; s is always disjoined from a following consonant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: cuer-da, chas-co, prpij-to; bas-ta, as-pi-rar, cons-pi-rar. When two consonants are separable, hyphenate between them; always separate initial s from the following consonant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greek syllabification rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Single consonants, consonant combinations that can begin a word, and mutes followed by p or b (or similar) are placed at the beginning of a syllable; other consonant combinations are divided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: place elements such as £-^o>, e-yw, e-tTTre-pa at syllable start; divide other clusters as in Trpatr-o-cu, eA.-7ris. Compound words are divided into their original parts, subject to the preceding rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Latin syllabification and compound separation
rubrics_metrics.description: A Latin word has as many syllables as vowels or diphthongs; divide before a single consonant between vowels; divide before the last consonant in clusters except for mute+liquid and qu/gu; separate compound words into component elements and apply rules within each element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Cae-sar, me-ri-di-es; om-nis, scrip-tus, cunc-tus (but pa-tris, e-quus, lin-gua). Compounds: ad-est, ab-rum-po, red-e-o, trans-i-go.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of superior figures for reference indexes
rubrics_metrics.description: For reference indexes (footnote markers) use superior figures as a rule; use other symbols (asterisks, daggers) only in special cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place index figures in the text after punctuation marks, without space, except in German where they are placed inside the punctuation. When figures are not used, the sequence should be: * (asterisk), † (dagger), ‡ (double dagger), § (section mark), || (parallels), ¶ (paragraph mark).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'ibid.' and related references
rubrics_metrics.description: When references to the same work follow each other closely and uninterruptedly, use 'ibid.' instead of repeating the title, but avoid using 'ibid.' as the first footnote on a verso page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If 'ibid.' would be the first footnote on a left-hand page, prefer repeating a short title or using loc. cit. (when referring to the entire citation) or op. cit. (when referring only to the work). Examples: 1 Spencer, Principles...; 2 Ibid.; 3 Ibid., chap. v.; 4 Spencer, loc. cit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Footnotes to tables formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Footnotes to tables should be set in 6-pt and placed at the foot of the table (not at the foot of the page). For reference indexes within tables use asterisks or similar symbols rather than superior figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 6-pt type for table footnotes. Refer back to general index-marker rules (see superior figures vs symbols). Ensure footnotes to tables remain within the table width.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omitting repeated author name in footnote
rubrics_metrics.description: If an author's name is given in the text in connection with a reference to or quotation from his work, omit repeating the name in the corresponding footnote.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: ...This theory is questioned by Herbert, as follows: 'I cannot admit ...' 1 Laws of the Ancients, I, 153. Do not repeat 'Herbert' in the footnote.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of index figure for quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: It is preferable to place the index (footnote) figure at the end of the quotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place the superscript/index figure after closing quotation punctuation when citing a quoted passage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviations and numeral conventions in references
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinarily omit 'Vol.,' 'chap.,' and 'p.' when referencing particular passages. Use Roman numerals (capitals) for Volume, Book, Part, Division; lower-case roman for chapters and introductory pages; Arabic numerals for numbers and text pages. For classical references use periods instead of commas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only use 'Vol.,' 'p.' etc. when confusion could arise. Examples: Miller, French Rev. II, Part IV, iii. Use appropriate punctuation conventions for classical works and modern English references as preferred by the author or editor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of publication date in periodical citations
rubrics_metrics.description: The date of publication in a reference to a periodical should immediately follow the volume number and be put in parentheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example formatting illustrated earlier in context; follow convention consistently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Footnote numbering conventions on linotype/monotype
rubrics_metrics.description: In linotype set works, footnotes should be numbered consecutively through an article (in a journal) or through a chapter (in a book) to avoid resetting; exceptions exist for some journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note exceptions: Botanical Gazette numbers footnotes consecutively through an article; the Astro-physical Journal has its own conventions. Check journal-specific style notes when preparing copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing: treatment of M', Me, Mac, St., Ste. prefixes
rubrics_metrics.description: Names beginning with M', Me, Mac, or St., Ste. should be listed as if the prefix were spelled Mac, Saint, Sainte so that users need not search multiple places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided: M'Intyre, Henry; Maclntyre, Thomas; list under 'Mac'/'Saint' forms as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing: compound and hyphenated names
rubrics_metrics.description: Compound names should be listed under the first part; list other parts in their alphabetical positions with cross-references. Hyphenated names gratuitously adopted (e.g., married women adding maiden names) may be disregarded and listed under the true name with a cross-reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Campbell-Bannerman, Sir Henry; Lloyd-George, David (and cross-ref: George, Lloyd-, David. See Lloyd-George.). For hyphenations by marriage, list under true name with cross-reference under the adopted form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing: prefixes and language-specific exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Names with prefixes should be listed under the part following the prefix, except in English (see compound rules), in French when prefix contains an article, in Italian/Spanish when prefix is simply the article, in Dutch where 'Van' etc. are capitalized, and when the prefix and name are written as one word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat naturalized names with prefixes according to the adopted language rules. Examples: Hoffman, von; Lima, de; Ponte e Horto, da; Santos Pereira Jardin, dos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing: umlaut handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Names spelled with umlaut a, o, u should be listed as if the umlaut were spelled out ae, oe, ue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Miiller, A. → list under 'Mu' as if Müller = Mueller; provide consistent spelling/entry to aid lookup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing: firms and multi-name entries with connectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Names or firms connected by 'and', '&', 'y', 'et', 'und', or 'e' should be listed according to the first letter of the name preceding the connective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Smith & Evans → under 'S'; Gomez y Pineda → under 'G'; Loubet et Meunier → under 'L'. Provide cross-references if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point-size conventions for tables
rubrics_metrics.description: In n-pt and 10-pt matter, open tables ordinarily set in 6-pt leaded; ruled in 8-pt solid. In 8-pt matter both open and ruled in 8-pt solid. In 8-pt matter open tables set in 6-pt leaded; ruled in 6-pt solid. In 6-pt matter both open and ruled set in 6-pt solid. Italic and bold-face figures may be used for columns representing totals/averages/percentages to set off result classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the specified table body type size relative to the surrounding text. See Table III illustration for examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Table captions and box-heads styling
rubrics_metrics.description: Captions for open-table columns and box-heads for ruled tables should ordinarily be set in 6-pt. Box-heads of open tables should be 6-pt caps and lower case unless subheads are used; then caps and small caps are used for the upper head and lower in caps and lower case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In ruled tables with multi-story box-heads, set primary heads in caps and small caps (except when second story is figures only); secondary in caps and lower case. Wherever small caps are used in box-heads, stub heading should usually also be caps and small caps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Table rule-to-matter spacing
rubrics_metrics.description: In ruled tables there should be at least two leads' space between horizontal rules and the enclosed matter, and (if practicable) at least the equivalent of an en quad between vertical rules and the matter enclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure adequate breathing room between rules and content: two leads (~2 points) vertically and an en quad horizontally if possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of leaders/periods between columns
rubrics_metrics.description: In open tables either periods, one em apart and aligned, or leaders may be used between columns. In ruled tables, leaders should usually be employed in the 'stub' if there is room, except where the stub runs over and a brace is necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A leader is a piece of type with dots (period leader) or short lines (hyphen leader). Use leaders to guide the eye where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting numeric columns in ruled tables
rubrics_metrics.description: In ruled columns of figures, use leaders to express blanks across the full column width; center the figures; if exact centering is not possible and digit groups vary, leave more space on the left; align all decimals and currency signs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Align decimal points and currency symbols vertically. For empty cells, use leaders spanning the column width.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading-matter in table columns
rubrics_metrics.description: When there is running text in table columns, center it if possible; if any line runs over, use hanging indentation and align all overflow lines on the left.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer centering for reading-matter but use hanging indents for wrapped lines so that overflow aligns consistently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Table rule usage and continuation
rubrics_metrics.description: Double rules should be used at the top of all tables; vertical double rules only when a table is doubled on itself and the stub is repeated. For continued broadside tables where heading is not repeated, use a single rule only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply double rules at table tops generally; use single rule for continued tables lacking repeated headings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open vs ruled tables and table-continuation consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Two-column tables should be set open; three or more columns should be ruled, except in special cases. All continuations of tables should have the same dimensions even if blank columns are necessary; tables with identical headings should be placed parallel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain consistent column dimensions across continuations; choose open or ruled format depending on column count and layout needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Table numbering, headlines, and footnote placement
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Table I,' etc., in table headlines should ordinarily be set in caps of the type used for the body and should not exceed the table width; a descriptive line follows in caps and small caps. A single descriptive headline without number should be caps in body type. Table footnotes should be in 6-pt with paragraph indentation and not exceed the table width; repeat footnotes on each page when tables with footnotes run over several pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using both 6-pt and 8-pt tables in the same work, use 8-pt headings over all tables. Repeat footnotes on continued pages for clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point system and pica standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The point is the underlying unit of typographical measures. The standard of measurement is the pica; a pica equals twelve points (one-sixth of an inch).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common named sizes and their point equivalents are listed (pica = 12-pt, small pica = 11-pt, long primer = 10-pt, bourgeois = 9-pt, brevier = 8-pt, minion = 7-pt, nonpareil = 6-pt, pearl = 5-pt). Use these as the standard scale for composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type styles definitions and manuscript indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinary type is called roman; italic is sloping face indicated in manuscripts by an underscore; bold face is heavy black indicated by a wavy line. A font includes caps, small caps, and lower-case letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the manuscript indication conventions: underline for italics, wavy line for bold; identify caps by three straight lines, small caps by two in manuscript markings. Examples show rendering in text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions of em, en, and related spaces
rubrics_metrics.description: An em (or em quad) is a square of type equal to the size of the type; an en quad is half an em. A three-em space (thick space) is one-third of an em and is standard for separating words. Four-em and five-em spaces are called middle and thin spaces; a hair-space is any space thinner than a five-em.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these measurements when specifying indents, dashes, and spacing. Examples of em/en dashes and hair spacing are provided for visual reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard spacing rules between words and punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: A standard line should have a 3-em space between most words and after commas; an en quad after semicolons and colons followed by a lower-case letter; two 3-em spaces after colons followed by a capital; an em quad after periods and final exclamation/interrogation points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These spacing conventions guide justification and interword spacing for well-spaced lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hierarchy for adjusting spacing to justify lines
rubrics_metrics.description: If spacing must be reduced, begin by tightening after commas and around slanting letters (letters with large shoulders); if increasing, begin with overlapping letters (kerns) and straight-up-and-down letters, and then use other punctuation in this order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain proportion: in a well-spaced line most words have 3-em spaces and the remainder not more than an en quad apart. Avoid following an exceptionally thin-spaced line with an exceptionally wide one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibitions on hair-spacing and last-line spacing
rubrics_metrics.description: Never hair-space or em-quad a line to avoid a run-over. Do not space out the last line of a paragraph leaving an indention of an em or more at the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid artificial squeezing or stretching of lines that harm overall texture; preserve uniformity across adjacent lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spacing rules for short words and special symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Short words like 'a' and 'an' should have the same space on each side. Use a thin space after §, f, and similar signs; before 'f.,' 'ff.,' and metric symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: '§ 14. Be it further ordained...' and 'pp. 10ff.; 16cm.' Maintain consistent micro-spacing around symbols for legibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spacing with currency and numeric symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: In American and English sums of money no space is used between the monetary symbol ($, £, s., d.) and the numerals; use an en leader for a decimal point in certain contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: $2.75; £1035. 2d.; 10°C. Follow local currency conventions and avoid inserting spaces between symbol and number.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spacing after numerals in headings and small-cap rules
rubrics_metrics.description: After Arabic and Roman numerals at the beginning of lines denoting subsections, place an en quad; after numerals at the beginning of center-heads, place an em quad. Small-cap headings should have an en quad between words; cap-and-small-cap and cap-headings two 3-em spaces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply consistent spacing to numeric lead-ins to headings and subsection markers to preserve visual rhythm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scripture reference spacing
rubrics_metrics.description: Scripture references should be spaced using a 9-unit colon (i.e., 'II Cor. i : 16-20; 2:5 — 3:12').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the specified spacing convention for scripture citations to ensure clarity and consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: No spaces before/around superscripts/subscripts in formulae
rubrics_metrics.description: Between letters forming products, and before superior (superscript) or inferior (subscript) figures or letters indicating powers, ordinarily no space should be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: j.x* = Sw2 (v2z2 — 2vwyz + 2W*y2). Keep mathematical expressions compact without additional spacing unless typographically required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indentation standards by measure and point size (linotype/monotype)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide standard paragraph indentations depending on measure width and type size. In linotype composition, indent all sizes 1 em in measures <10 picas; provide specific em/point indent values for other measure ranges. In monotype, indent so all paragraph indents align regardless of size, with suggested standards for measures of 19–30 picas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: For measures 10–20 picas: 12-pt indent 1½ ems; 10-pt 1½; 9-pt 1¼; 8-pt 1¼; 6-pt 2 ems. Hanging indents also have recommended values by measure. Narrower or wider measures should be indented proportionally less or more. Use poetry-specific rules: center longest line, align by rhyme/lengths as detailed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraph style guidance (plain vs hanging)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish two kinds of paragraphs: plain (first line indented, others flush) and hanging (first line flush, others indented). Plain paragraphs are preferable for ordinary reading-matter; use hanging indention when emphasizing opening words/numbers or for long center-heads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply plain paragraphs as default; use hanging indent for lists, extended headings, or to bring opening words into relief. See examples for usage and exceptions (poetry, quotations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Leads and slugs definitions and usage
rubrics_metrics.description: A lead is a strip of metal separating lines of type; ordinary (standard) lead is 2 points thick. Matter with leads is called leaded; without leads, solid. A slug is a strip thicker than a lead used in make-up; standard slug sizes are 6 and 12 points thick.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use leads to control interline spacing; slugs for spacing after headlines, etc. Typical practice is to set books leaded; use solid setting sparingly (e.g., index).

rubrics_metrics.name: Head and heading conventions (center-head, side-head, cut-in, box-head, running-head)
rubrics_metrics.description: Center-head: headline centered, usually set in caps or small caps and not followed by a period; use 'pyramid' or 'hanging indention' for multi-line center-heads. Side-head: at side of column, set flush or run-in, often in italics with only first word and proper names capitalized, or in caps and small caps or bold. Cut-in head: placed in a box cut into side of type-page under first two lines. Box-head: head for a column in a ruled table. Running-head: placed at top of each page, centered, usually two point sizes smaller than body text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the typographic conventions for each head type. Center multi-line heads with pyramid/hanging formats; use appropriate capitalization and type style for side-heads and running-heads. Set running-heads in roman or italic capitals two sizes smaller than body text for good proportion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof types and correction workflow
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions of proof stages: galley-proof (type in galley), page-proof (type made into page form), plate-proof/foundry-proof (proof before electrotype cast, with black border), foul proof (galley-proof containing author's corrections), and revise (new proof corrected from a marked proof).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the specified proof nomenclature to manage correction cycles and to identify which stage the material is in; be aware plate-proofs have distinctive borders and that most publications print from plates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make-up and folio placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Make-up is the arranging of type-lines into page-form. A folio is a page-number: even numbers on verso (left), odd on recto (right). A drop-folio is a page-number placed at the bottom of a page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange make-up according to folio conventions; ensure page numbering placement follows the even/odd placement rule for consistency across the book.
